Learn to explain how to talk about choosing whether an async function stays on the caller's actor or runs in the background: @concurrent, Nonisolated Nonsending & Caller Isolation, with real code, a quiz at the end and each example read twice (normal, then slow).

Today's terms
@concurrent - An attribute that makes an async function run off the caller's actor, on the background pool.
Nonisolated Nonsending - A mode for an async function that keeps it running on the caller's actor instead of hopping away.
Caller Isolation - The actor a function was called from, which a nonsending async function keeps using.

landscape.hook: Can you explain @concurrent, Nonisolated Nonsending and Caller Isolation in English?

dialogue.title: Where does my async function run?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Jake, my screen freezes when I call `crunch` from the main actor.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Is `crunch` heavy? Mark it @concurrent, so it runs off the main actor.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: So @concurrent moves the work to the background pool?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Yes. It does not run on the actor that called it.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: And what about `load`? It is only a quick async call.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Keep it nonisolated nonsending. It does not hop away from the actor.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: So it runs on the main actor, because `show` called it?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Right. It uses the caller isolation, so there is no data race and no hop.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: I thought every async function left the actor.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: That was the old rule. With nonsending, the caller isolation stays.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: OK. @concurrent for heavy work, nonisolated nonsending for light work.
